                    ### Question
                    A 38-year-old man consulted for dyspnea and hemoptysis. Blood tests have creatinine 7 mg / dl, urea 250 mg / dl and anti-MBG (anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies) positive high titer. A renal biopsy was performed, showing crescents in 75% of the glomeruli, and in the immunofluorescence a linear Ig deposition pattern appeared. Which of the following is the correct answer?

                    ### Options
                    opa. It is an Ig A Nephropathy with acute renal failure.
opb. The performance of plasmapheresis would be indicated.
opc. It is a membranous glomerulonephritis.
opd. Mycophenolate mofetil is the initial treatment of choice.
ope. Glomerular involvement is caused by the presence of circulating immune complexes.

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The clinical presentation of dyspnea, hemoptysis, high creatinine, and positive anti-GBM antibodies, along with renal biopsy findings of crescents in 75% of glomeruli and linear Ig deposition, is consistent with anti-GBM disease, also known as Goodpasture's syndrome. This condition is characterized by the presence of anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies leading to glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage. The standard treatment involves plasmapheresis to remove circulating antibodies and immunosuppression, typically with corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide. Mycophenolate mofetil is not the initial treatment of choice. The evidence paths confirm that plasmapheresis is a treatment for anti-GBM disease, aligning with the consensus that it is indicated in this scenario. The presence of linear Ig deposition and anti-GBM antibodies rules out IgA nephropathy and membranous glomerulonephritis, and the disease is not caused by circulating immune complexes, but rather by direct antibody-mediated damage.
